Wipro Limited :

General

The first objection put forth by the assessee before the Tribunal was that the administration support service and marketing support services were rendered by the assessee to one of its AEs, CSS BV - India BO. The said AE was assessed to tax in India as it had a PE in India. In such assessment in the case of the AE, this transaction was accepted without any adjustment. Besides the above, it was pointed out that the assessee rendered services to another group company CISCO Systems Capital (I) Pvt. Ltd. The said company was covered by the provisions of section 40A(2)(b), but the Assessing Officer did not make any disallowance of the payments made to the assessed tax, invoking the provisions of section 40A(2)(a). The above facts cannot be the basis to come to the conclusion that the payments made to the assessee for administration support services and marketing support services by its AE is at arm's length. In view of the provisions of section 92, any transaction with AE has to pass the arm's length price test, therefore, the above contentions raised by the assessee are rejected as not relevant. [Para 51]

Further, the approach adopted by the TPO of combining the Administrative Support services and management/marketing services and making a comparison of the combined results has to be upheld as both the segments were inter connected.

Now, it is necessary to deal with the comparability of each of the companies and their comparability with that of the assessee. [Para 52]

Companies chosen by the assessee in its administative and other support services

Hindustan Housing Company Ltd.: This company is engaged in providing administrative services, house keeping services and other administration support services to Bajaj group of companies of which it is apart. This company has related party transactions to the extent of 88.23 per cent and cannot be regarded as a comparable. [Para 53.1]

IDC India Ltd. : This company is in the business of market research and management consultancy. This company can be regarded as a comparable. In this regard, it is opined that the administration support services and management support services are akin to management services and this company should be considered as a comparable. [Para 53.2]

New Age Entertainment Ltd.: This company is in the entertainment industry and renders distribution of marketing of motion pictures. This company, cannot be regarded as a comparable as the functions performed are entirely different. [Para 53.3]

Office Care Services Ltd.: This company renders house keeping maintenance work and manpower support services, which are not akin to the nature of services performed by the assessee and therefore was rightly rejected by the TPO. [Para 53.4]

Forbes Facility Services Pvt. Ltd.: This company renders to its holding company mechanized house keeping and providing integrated facility services. The nature of the industry being different and the nature of services to be performed being routine upkeep of products sold, it cannot be considered as comparable with that of the assessee. [Para 53.5]

Competent Automobiles Company Ltd.: This company is in the automobile sector. The assessee has taken the segmental results of the services and spare parts division. This company cannot be considered as a comparable. [Para 53.6]

DLF Services Ltd.: This company is a group company of DLF Ltd. and is in the business of providing services facility management to clients of commercial complexes. Empire Industries Ltd.: This company has operations in manufacturing division, trading and indenting division, educational programmes division and others. PAE Ltd.: This company is in the business of distribution of lead acid storage batteries to provide power storage in power back-up systems. This company cannot be regarded as a comparable. [Para 53.11]

The Tribunal in Hyundai Motor India Engg. (P.) Ltd. (supra) observed that the company Informed Technologies is also providing ITES and back office BPO services and in the column of segmental reporting, it is stated that the company is provisionally engaged in the business process outsources which is only reportable as per AS-17 standard issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India on segmental reporting. Thus, this company can be considered as a comparable. Further, the Transfer Pricing Officer has not mentioned about the filter of operating revenue being more than 75 per cent. Therefore, the Dispute Resolution Panel is clearly in error in considering the same. The Transfer Pricing Officer is directed to consider this company as a comparable after verifying the details furnished by the assessee. [Para 12]

In the instant case, the assessee has been treated as an ITES back office service provider and even in the case of Hyundai Motor India Engg. (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2019] 102 taxmann.com 10 (Hyd. - Trib.), the assessee has been considered as an ITES service provider and the assessment year involved in the appeal in the instant case as well as in the appeal of Hyundai Motor India Engg. (P.) Ltd. (supra). It is also observed that the comparables taken by the Transfer Pricing Officer are exactly the same. Therefore, the decision taken in the case of Hyundai Motor India Engg. (P.) Ltd. (supra) would also apply to the assessee. In the said case it was held that the activities of Capgemini Business are much more diversified than the activities of the assessee and unless and until a suitable adjustment can be made, the said company cannot be taken as a comparable. It has been held in a number of cases that where a comparable is into diversified activities, the same can be taken as a comparable provided the segmental results are available. It is observed that the segmental results are not available for ITES services. Therefore, Capgemini Business is to be excluded from the final list of comparables.

As regards Hartron Communications Ltd. is concerned it was observed that before the Transfer Pricing Officer, the assessee had only taken an objection that the said company is functionally dissimilar. Before the Dispute Resolution Panel also, the assessee had also stated that in addition to the BPO, LPO and ITES services, this company is also engaged in providing Intellectual Property services in the nature of patent search, patent protection, and obtaining the trade-mark services, IP Management and, further, in software development services such as Web page Application, Standalone Software Application, Distributed Applications, Desktop/Laptop Applications and Mobile Applications. The assessee had relied upon the Annual Report as well as the website information of the said company to submit as above and pleaded that no segmental information is available. However, the Dispute Resolution Panel has summarily rejected the assessee's contention and has confirmed the assessment order. Since the facts mentioned by the assessee about Hartron Communications need to be verified, it is deemed fit and proper to remit the issue to the file of the Assessing Officer for verification of the assessee's contentions. Thus, it is held that if the company is found to be in diversified activities and no segmental information is available, then this company cannot be taken as a comparable. [Para 10]

Following the same, the Assessing Officer is to be directed to exclude these two companies from the final list of comparables. [Para 11]

(supra), it was held that Infosys BPO, be excluded from the final set of comparables.[Para 6.3.1]

BNR Udyog (Seg-Medical Transcription) It was found that the benchmarking of 'BNR' has been done only at the medical transcription segment and issue of RPT has not been urged before the Assessing Officer/DRP. TCS E-serve ('TCS')

It was observed that while the assessee has contended that the services rendered by this company, are high end KPO services, it has not brought out as to which of these are the services that would come under technical services. On the other hand, it was noticed that the TPO has held all the services rendered by the assessee to be BPO services without any proper analysis. (supra) has remanded the matter of comparability of this company to the file of the TPO for fresh consideration. Excel Infoways (Seg-IT/BPO) ('Excel')

Similar is the position with regard to volatility of profits/peculiarity of economic circumstances. Comparable Infosys BPO Ltd.

In assessment year 2008-09, this comparable was excluded as an extraordinary event took place in that year. Infosys BPO Limited acquired skill sets in the finance, administration space as well as enhanced its global presence with centers at Thailand and Poland. In course of hearing, the assessee filed the news item in the Economic Times, wherein, as regards the acquisition of Australia-based Portland Group for AUD 37 mn, it is pointed out that the deal would essentially enable Infosys BPO to have a reach into the Australian market and will enhance their sourcing and procurement capabilities. It is further stated that Infosys' focus on value-added services and this will add to it. Further, it was stated therein that Portland Group has over 100 employees with a reported revenue of approximately A $ 31.3 million for the fiscal year ended 30-6-2011. Further, Portland Group has over 100 procurement specialists with domain expertise and some 40-odd clients. Thus, the deal certainly helped Infosys BPO to intensify its services offerings and took sourcing and procurement functions to a higher level. Thus, it cannot be said that though the deal was struck in January, 2012 but could not impact the profitability of assessee particularly when the Portland Group had substantial presence over area and had specialized skills. Therefore, this event definitely would affect the profitability of Infosys BPO which increased substantially. Further, assessee has also demonstrated various aspects, noted earlier, which clearly distinguished Infosys BPO from assessee and, therefore, this comparable be excluded from the list of comparables. Comparable BNR Udyog Ltd.

On the contrary, as noted above, the services rendered by the assessee under the ITeS segment are primarily in the nature of database administration and management, operating systems, and network administration. In this regard, the assessee has made relevant segment reporting in the notes to its financial statements. Therefore, it is evident that this company is earning income from various business activities including income from the sale of products/license fees without any operating segment which is functionally comparable to the assessee. Accordingly, the TPO Assessing Officer should exclude said company while benchmarking the international transaction pertaining to 'Provision of IT support and related services. [Para 14]

Comparable XS Cad India Private Ltd.

From the segmental reporting in Note 23(v) to the financial statement of this company, the segmental reporting of the company is based on the geographical location of the customer and accordingly country-wise, namely for USA, Canada, Australia, UK, Germany, and India reporting has been made by this company. Further, the company treats its complete operations as a single segment, i.e. 'Information Technology Services'. As the assessee has made relevant segment reporting in the notes to its financial statements but this company is earning revenue from various streams, in the absence of relevant segmental information, this company cannot be said to be functionally comparable to the assessee. This company has claimed to be a leading player offering customised software, digital transformation and enterprise mobility solutions for clients across the globe. It is also claimed that Infobeans Technologies Ltd. provides software engineering services primarily in Custom Application Development, Content Management Systems, Enterprise Mobility, and Big Data Analytics. In the annual report, it is claimed that this company earned 99.26 per cent of its total turnover from computer programming, consultancy, and related activities. The entire revenue from operations, in the financial statement of this company, comprises of income from software services, without any further bifurcation of this revenue and segmental information. Before the DRP the assessee raised this objection that no segmented financials of this company are available. Further, this fact was also accepted by the DRP that this company has only one segment, i.e. sale of software. However, the DRP proceeded to reject the objections filed by the assessee and held this company to be comparable to the assessee. Therefore, in the absence of relevant segmental information, this company cannot be held to be functionally comparable to the assessee. BNR Udyog Ltd. (Segment - Medical Transcription) The contentions of the assessee that the company BNR Udyog Ltd., is functionally different and fails the RPT filter at the entity level. It is found from the record that the benchmarking of selected company 'BNR' has been done only at the medical transcription segment and issue of RPT has not been urged before the Assessing Officer/DRP. From a perusal of the decision of the co-ordinate bench of this Tribunal in the case of Indegene (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2017] 85 taxmann.com 60 for asst. year 2012-13, the issue of comparability of 'BNR' has been remanded to the file for the TPO for fresh consideration on ground that in the year under consideration, there are 3 segments. How much of the RPT expenses pertain to each of the segments requires examination and this aspect had not been analyzed by either the TPO or the assessee. While it is clear from the TPO's order that if the benchmarking is done only for the medical transcription segment, then the RPT pertaining to that segment only should be considered. However, since how much of the RPT pertain to the medical transcription segment has not been determined by either the TPO or the assessee, we deem it appropriate and proper to remand the matter of comparability of this company BNR Udyog Ltd., to the file of the TPO for determination of the issue afresh in line with observation above. Following the above decision of the co-ordinate bench in the case of Indegene (P.) Ltd. (supra) and considering the factual matrix involved, that how much RPT pertains to the medical transcription has not been determined by either the TPO or the assessee, it is appropriate and proper to remand the issue of comparability of this company, BNR Udyog Ltd. to the file of the TPO for determination afresh. Similar is the position with regard to volatility of profits/peculiarity of economic circumstances. In this view of the matter, it is appropriate to remand the issue of comparability of this company, Excel Infoways back to the file of the TPO for examination and verification of the assessee's contentions on the issue of abnormality of profits and of failing of the employees cost filter of 25 per cent at segmental level, for which the Assessing Officer may gather information under section 133(6). The "Translation Charges" paid comprises of 40% of the translation income of INR.5,45,41,023 which represented outsourced activity. Therefore, Cosmic Global is functionally different and this aspect has not been adjudicated by the DRP. He submitted that this comparable was excluded as a comparable for ITeS companies in the following rulings owing to different functional profile and business model:

a.

Xchanging Technology Services India (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2015] 57 taxmann.com 437 - Delhi ITAT Confirmed by the High Court of Delhi in ITA No. 813/2015 on 20.10.2015;

b.

Xchanging Technology Services India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2015] 60 taxmann.com 389 - Delhi ITAT - Confirmed by the High Court of Delhi in ITA No. 36/2016 on 19.01.2016

c.

Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 60 taxmann.com 355/234 Taxman 573/377 ITR 533 (Delhi) - Delhi High Court

d.

Parexel International (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2014] 51 taxmann.com 238 (Hyd. - Trib.)

e.

Cummins Turbo Technologies Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2016] 68 taxmann.com 273 (Pune - Trib.) ITAT and hence pleaded to exclude the same .

3.1 On Fortune Infotech Limited, the AR submitted that this company was subject to Extraordinary events; 2 Consistently fails RPT filter;&3. Develops and owns unique web based software for niche services.

(a)

On Extraordinary event, the AR submitted that during the Fy 2009-10, Fortune had merged with other entities and also sold its entire investment in its wholly owned subsidiary 'Fortune Infotech USA, Inc. In this regard, the AR placed reliance in the following cases wherein this company has been rejected on the ground of extra ordinary events:

a.

Symphony Marketing Solutions India (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2013] 38 taxmann.com 55 (Bang. - Trib.)

b.

Capital IQ Information Systems India (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2013] 32 taxmann.com 21/57 SOT 14 (URO) (Hyd. - Trib.)

(b)

On Use of unique software, the AR submitted that this company has developed and owns its unique web based software by which it provides niche services to its customers. Therefore, this company cannot be taken as comparable with ITES entities having little or no intangibles of their own and placed reliance on the following decisions:

a.

RR Donnelley India Outsource (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2016] 75 taxmann.com 306 (Chennai - Trib.);

b.

24/7 Customer.com (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2012] 28 taxmann.com 258/[2013] 140 ITD 344 (Bang.)

c.

ITeS company and it had not outsourced its services. Hence, Vishal Information Tech was not a suitable comparable. In support of this argument, the Ld. Counsel relied on the Ld. CIT(A)'s order in the assessee's own case for AY 2008-09, where the Ld. CIT(A) had excluded this company on similar ground. The Ld. DR placed reliance on Ld. TPO's findings in respect of this company. 48. We have heard both parties and have perused the material available on the record. After careful consideration of material on the record and facts in entirety, we do not find force in the argument of the Ld. Counsel that Vishal Information Tech. Ltd. is having any functional dissimilarities. The dissimilarities pointed out by the Ld. Counsel is only that this comparable has outsourced its ITeS, whereas the assessee not. After careful consideration of material on the record and facts in entirety, the profit margin arisen toVishal Information Tech. Ltd. should be lower being high cost of outsourced services than the assessee's inhouse cost for similar services. However, it is not so. That is why the upward adjustment in ALP has taken place on this score.This comparable is found engaged in similar ITeS in the relevant year. In view of the above, we hold that the Ld. CIT(A) is justified in retaining/including Vishal Information Tech. Ltd.in the final set of comparables. We therefore, do not find any infirmity in the impugned order in respect of this comparable. We therefore, decline to interfere with the finding of the Ld. CIT(A) in this regard. Accordingly, Vishal Information Tech. Ltd.is held validly included in the list of final comparables.

50. The above finding in para 26 [SDS Segment] is held applicable mutatis mutandisin this comparable also. We therefore, direct the AO/TPO to exclude Wipro Ltd. (segmental)from the final set of comparables in this segment also.

FOR AY 2008-09

51. The assessee has chosen TNMM on a segmental basis as the most appropriate method for both segments i.e. SDS and ITeS Segment and Operating Profit by Operating Cost as the profit level indicator ("PLI"), which, in principle, has been accepted by the AO/TPO for benchmarking the assessee's international transactions. However, the TPO has added/modified comparables by taking different/modified filters. The TPO selected 19 comparables for SDS Segment and 20 for ITeS segment. For SDS Segment, the TPO took (i) 6comparables out of the Assessee's TP Study and (ii) 13 new comparables chosen by the TPO after modifying filters for selection of comparables. For ITeS Segment, the TPO took (i) 4comparables out of the Assessee's TP Study and (ii) 16 new comparables chosen by the TPO after modifying filters for selection of comparables. The facts of this case are almost similar to that of the AY 2007-08. All comparables selected by the TPO for AY 2008-09 are identical to those selected in AY 2007-08, except for one comparable: Infosys BPO Ltd. Aggrieved by the order of the AO/TPO, the assessee filed an appeal before the Ld. CIT(A), who rejected few comparables.

SDS segment

52. In the SDS segment, the Revenue has challenged the exclusion of Infosys Technologies Ltd., Wipro Ltd. (seg), Celestial Biolabs, Flextronics Software Systems Ltd. and I-Gate Global Solutions Ltd., while the assessee, vide its CO, has challenged the inclusion of Avani Cimcom Technologies Ltd. and Kals Information Systems Ltd. Both Ld. Representatives were fare enough to admit that except Flextronics Software Systems Ltd. and I-Gate Global Solutions Ltd., the disputed comparables in AY 2008-09 were identical to those considered in AY 2007-08 and thus, they requested to consider theirabove-mentioned arguments/submissions/contentions of AY 2007-08 in AY 2008-09 as well.

53. We have heard both parties. The above findings in the comparables; namely, Infosys Technologies Ltd., Wipro Ltd. (seg), Celestial Biolabs, Avani Cimcom Technologies Ltd. and Kals Information Systems Ltd. are held applicable mutatis mutandis in these comparables in AY 2008-09also. We therefore, direct the AO/TPO to excludethese comparable from the final set of comparables accordingly.

54. The Revenue has challenged the exclusion of Flextronics Software Systems Ltd. and I-Gate Global Solutions Ltd from the list of comparables in SDS Segment.

Indian Accounting Standard (Ind AS 108)

Operating Segments

(This Indian Accounting Standard includes paragraphs set in bold type and plain type, which have equal authority. Paragraphs in bold type indicate the main principles.)

Core principle

1. An entity shall disclose information to enable users of its financial statements to evaluate the nature and financial effects of the business activities in which it engages and the economic environments in which it operates.

Scope

2. This Accounting Standard shall apply to companies to which Indian Accounting Standards (Ind ASs) notified under the Companies Act apply.

[Refer Appendix 1]

3. If an entity that is not required to apply this Ind AS chooses to disclose information about segments that does not comply with this Ind AS, it shall not describe the information as segment information.

4. If a financial report contains both the consolidated financial statements of a parent that is within the scope of this Ind AS as well as the parent's separate financial statements, segment information is required only in the consolidated financial statements.

Operating segments

5. An operating segment is a component of an entity:

(a)

that engages in business activities from which it may earn revenues and incur expenses (including revenues and expenses relating to transactions with other components of the same entity),

(b)

whose operating results are regularly reviewed by the entity's chief operating decision maker to make decisions about resources to be allocated to the segment and assess its performance, and

(c)

for which discrete financial information is available.

An operating segment may engage in business activities for which it has yet to earn revenues, for example, start-up operations may be operating segments before earning revenues.

6. Not every part of an entity is necessarily an operating segment or part of an operating segment. For example, a corporate headquarters or some functional departments may not earn revenues or may earn revenues that are only incidental to the activities of the entity and would not be operating segments. For the purposes of this Ind AS, an entity's post-employment benefit plans are not operating segments.

7. The term 'chief operating decision maker' identifies a function, not necessarily a manager with a specific title. That function is to allocate resources to and assess the performance of the operating segments of an entity. Often the chief operating decision maker of an entity is its chief executive officer or chief operating officer but, for example, it may be a group of executive directors or others.

8. For many entities, the three characteristics of operating segments described in paragraph 5 clearly identify its operating segments. However, an entity may produce reports in which its business activities are presented in a variety of ways. If the chief operating decision maker uses more than one set of segment information, other factors may identify a single set of components as constituting an entity's operating segments, including the nature of the business activities of each component, the existence of managers responsible for them, and information presented to the board of directors.

9. Generally, an operating segment has a segment manager who is directly accountable to and maintains regular contact with the chief operating decision maker to discuss operating activities, financial results, forecasts, or plans for the segment. The term 'segment manager' identifies a function, not necessarily a manager with a specific title. The chief operating decision maker also may be the segment manager for some operating segments. A single manager may be the segment manager for more than one operating segment. If the characteristics in paragraph 5 apply to more than one set of components of an organisation but there is only one set for which segment managers are held responsible, that set of components constitutes the operating segments.

10. The characteristics in paragraph 5 may apply to two or more overlapping sets of components for which managers are held responsible. That structure is sometimes referred to as a matrix form of organisation. For example, in some entities, some managers are responsible for different product and service lines worldwide, whereas other managers are responsible for specific geographical areas. The chief operating decision maker regularly reviews the operating results of both sets of components, and financial information is available for both. In that situation, the entity shall determine which set of components constitutes the operating segments by reference to the core principle.

Reportable segments

11. An entity shall report separately information about each operating segment that:

(a)

has been identified in accordance with paragraphs 5–10 or results from aggregating two or more of those segments in accordance with paragraph 12, and

(b)

exceeds the quantitative thresholds in paragraph 13.

Paragraphs 14–19 specify other situations in which separate information about an operating segment shall be reported.

Appendix A

Defined term

This Appendix is an integral part of the Ind AS. Appendix 1

Note: This Appendix is not a part of the Indian Accounting Standard. The purpose of this Appendix is only to bring out the major differences, if any, between Indian Accounting Standard (Ind AS) 108 and the corresponding International Financial Reporting Standard (IFRS) 8, Operating Segments, issued by the International Accounting Standards Board.

Comparison with IFRS 8, Operating Segments

1. The transitional provisions given in IFRS 108 has not been given in Ind AS 108, since all transitional provisions related to Ind ASs, wherever considered appropriate, have been included in Ind AS 101, First-time Adoption of Indian Accounting Standards, corresponding to IFRS 1, First-time Adoption of International Financial Reporting Standards.

2. Different terminology is used, as used in existing laws eg, the term 'balance sheet' is used instead of 'Statement of financial position' and 'Statement of profit and loss' is used instead of 'Statement of comprehensive income'.

3. Paragraph 2 of IFRS 8 requires that the standard shall apply to :

(a)

the separate or individual financial statements of an entity:

(i)

whose debt or equity instruments are traded in a public market (a domestic or foreign stock exchange or an over-the-counter market, including local and regional markets), or

(ii)

that files, or is in the process of filing, its financial statements with a securities commission or other regulatory organisation for the purpose of issuing any class of instruments in a public market; and

(b)

the consolidated financial statements of a group with a parent:

(i)

whose debt or equity instruments are traded in a public market (a domestic or foreign stock exchange or an over-the-counter market, including local and regional markets), or

(ii)

that files, or is in the process of filing, the consolidated financial statements with a securities commission or other regulatory organisation for the purpose of issuing any class of instruments in a public market.

The above have been deleted in the Ind AS as the applicability or exemptions to the Indian Accounting Standards is governed by the Companies Act and the Rules made thereunder. However, the paragraph number has been retained in Ind AS 108 to maintain consistency with paragraph numbers of IFRS 8.

If an entity changes the structure of its internal organisation in a manner that causes the composition of its reportable segments to change, the corresponding information for earlier periods, including interim periods, shall be restated unless the information is not available and the cost to develop it would be excessive. Following a change in the composition of its reportable segments, an entity shall disclose whether it has restated the corresponding items of segment information for earlier periods.

Appendix 1

Note: This Appendix is not a part of the Indian Accounting Standard. The purpose of this Appendix is only to bring out the major differences, if any, between Indian Accounting Standard (Ind AS) 33 and the corresponding International Accounting Standard (IAS) 33, Earnings per Share, issued by the International Accounting Standards Board.

Comparison with IAS 33, Earnings per Share

1. IAS 33 provides that when an entity presents both consolidated financial statements and separate financial statements, it may give EPS related information in consolidated financial statements only, whereas, the Ind AS 33 requires EPS related information to be disclosed both in consolidated financial statements and separate financial statements.

2. Different terminology is used, as used in existing laws eg, the term 'Statement of profit and loss' is used instead of 'Statement of comprehensive income'. The words 'approval of the financial statements for issue' have been used instead of 'authorisation of the financial statements for issue' in the context of financial statements considered for the purpose of events after the reporting period.

3. Paragraph 2 of IAS 33 requires that the entire standard applies to:

(a)

the separate or individual financial statements of an entity:

(i)

whose ordinary shares or potential ordinary shares are traded in a public market (a domestic or foreign stock exchange or an over-the-counter market, including local and regional markets) or

(ii)

that files, or is in the process of filing, its financial statements with a Securities Regulator or other regulatory organisation for the purpose of issuing ordinary shares in a public market; and

(b)

the consolidated financial statements of a group with a parent:

(i)

whose ordinary shares or potential ordinary shares are traded in a public market (a domestic or foreign stock exchange or an over-the-counter market, including local and regional markets) or

(ii)

that files, or is in the process of filing, its financial statements with a Securities Regulator or other regulatory organisation for the purpose of issuing ordinary shares in a public market.

It also requires that an entity that discloses earnings per share shall calculate and disclose earnings per share in accordance with this Standard.

The above have been deleted in the Ind AS as the applicability or exemptions to theIndASs is governed by the Companies Act and the Rules made thereunder. However, the paragraph number has been retained in Ind AS 33 to maintain consistency with paragraph numbers of IAS 33.

4. Paragraph 4 has been modified in Ind AS 33 to clarify that an entity shall not present in separate financial statements, earnings per share based on the information given in consolidated financial statements, besides requiring as in IAS 33, that earnings per share based on the information given in separate financial statements shall not be presented in the consolidated financial statements.

5. In Ind AS 33, a paragraph has been added after paragraph 12 on the following lines:

"Where any item of income or expense which is otherwise required to be recognized in profit or loss in accordance with accounting standards is debited or credited to securities premium account/other reserves, the amount in respect thereof shall be deducted from profit or loss from continuing operations for the purpose of calculating basic earnings per share."

6. In Ind AS 33, paragraph 15 has been amended by adding the phrase, 'irrespective of whether such discount or premium is debited or credited to securities premium account in view of requirements of any law' to further clarify that such discount or premium shall also be amortised to retained earnings.

7. Requirements regarding disclosure of amounts per share using a reported component, basic and diluted earnings per share and basic and diluted earnings per share for discontinued operations in the separate income statement, where separate income statement is presented under following paragraphs of IAS 33 have been deleted:

(i)

paragraph 4A

Illustration II

Illustration on Determination of Reportable Segments [Paragraphs 27-29]

This illustration does not form part of the Accounting Standard. Its purpose is to illustrate the application of paragraphs 27-29 of the Accounting Standard.

An enterprise operates through eight segments, namely, A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H. The relevant information about these segments is given in the following table (amounts in Rs.'000): The reportable segments of the enterprise will be identified as below:

(a)

In accordance with paragraph 27(a), segments whose total revenue from external sales and inter-segment sales is 10% or more of the total revenue of all segments, external and internal, should be identified as reportable segments. Therefore, Segments A and B are reportable segments.

(b)

As per the requirements of paragraph 27(b), it is to be first identified whether the combined result of all segments in profit or the combined result of all segments in loss is greater in absolute amount. From the table, it is evident that combined result in loss (i.e., Rs.100,000) is greater. Therefore, the individual segment result as a percentage of Rs.100,000 needs to be examined. In accordance with paragraph 27(b), Segments B and C are reportable segments as their segment result is more than the threshold limit of 10%.

(c)

Segments A, B and D are reportable segments as per paragraph 27(c), as their segment assets are more than 10% of the total segment assets.

Thus, Segments A, B, C and D are reportable segments in terms of the criteria laid down in paragraph 27. Paragraph 28 of the Standard gives an option to the management of the enterprise to designate any segment as a reportable segment. In the given case, it is presumed that the management decides to designate Segment E as a reportable segment. Paragraph 29 requires that if total external revenue attributable to reportable segments identified as aforesaid constitutes less than 75% of the total enterprise revenue, additional segments should be identified as reportable segments even if they do not meet the 10% thresholds in paragraph 27, until at least 75% of total enterprise revenue is included in reportable segments.

The total external revenue of Segments A, B, C, D and E, identified above as reportable segments, is Rs. 295,000. This is less than 75% of total enterprise revenue of Rs. 400,000. The management of the enterprise is required to designate any one or more of the remaining segments as reportable segment(s) so that the external revenue of reportable segments is at least 75% of the total enterprise revenue. Suppose, the management designates Segment H for this purpose. Now the external revenue of reportable segments is more than 75% of the total enterprise revenue. Segments A, B, C, D, E and H are reportable segments. Segments F and G will be shown as reconciling items.

With nine rounds of transfer pricing audit completed in January 2014, the challenging days for Indian outsourcing sector does not seem to get over. The total quantum of transfer pricing adjustments made in FY 2012-13 was to the tune of seventy thousand crores1 (for Assessment Year ("AY") 2009-10) up by 54 per cent earlier. Indian outsourcing sector accounts for more than half the total claims in transfer pricing adjustments made during the aforesaid audit cycle from about one-third earlier.

However, as per recently disseminated data, the additions to income of companies undertaking international transaction has dropped by over 14 per cent to sixty thousand crores2 in FY 2014 tax audit cycle (for AY 2010-11). This seems to be a silver lining in an otherwise dismal environment emanating from the North Block.

Outsourcing sector accounts for more than USD 100 billion share in India's economy with big foreign companies like IBM, Capgemini, Microsoft, GE etc. putting forward a big basket of service offerings viz. customer service, risk and fraud management and finance and accounting. In the backdrop of the great demographic dividend, India has been one of the most preferred Knowledge Services Outsourcing ("KSO") destinations holding 70 per-cent share of the global KSO market3. India is poised to emerge as a global hub for KSO by 2015.

Over a period of time, multiplicity of business arrangements have happened in the outsourcing space starting from outsourcing of accounting processes to legal and research process outsourcing. While, Business Process Outsourcing ("BPO") service stands for taking up routine operations like data entry, voice calling and accounting services, a shift of functions performed that requires expert analysis and decision making viz. patent application drafting, technical research and advisory activities etc. mark the outset of a new category of Knowledge Process Outsourcing ("KPO") services. This broad bifurcation though coined by the industry itself is important from a transfer pricing stand-point and is analyzed deeply by the Special Bench of Mumbai Tribunal in the case of Maersk Global Centres (India) Private Limited discussed in this article.

Being a booming sector, Indian Information Technology ecosystem comprises of many aces to the likes of Infosys, Wipro, Tata Consultancy and other big Indian players. In such backdrop, how adequate would it be to compare margins of smaller IT companies with the abnormal margins of aforesaid gigantic companies having global business outshoots also, is another vexatious TP issue dealt with in detail in the aforesaid judgment.

1. FACTS OF CASE

Maersk Global Centres (India) Private Limited ("Maersk India") was incorporated in India as a wholly owned subsidiary of Maersk GSC Holdings, part of Maersk Group. Maersk India is in the business of shared services and renders transaction processing support and information technology services. During the year under assessment, Maersk India provided certain IT and IT enabled services to its Associated Enterprises ("AEs") and separately benchmarked the aforesaid transactions under IT and ITeS business segments. Applying Transactional Net Margin Method ("TNMM") with operating profit to total cost ("OP/TC") as Profit level indicator ("PLI"), the assessee selected thirteen comparables and claimed working capital and risk adjustment in its TP report.

In case of ITeS segment, the TPO classified the services provided by Maersk India as KPO services and rejected all but one comparables selected by the assessee and modified the search criteria adopted by assessee. He selected seven comparables including one chosen by the assessee. TPO allowed working capital adjustment but dismissed risk adjustment. In case of IT service segment, TPO computed arm's length margin without allowing working capital adjustment. The AO maintained the TPOs views in the draft assessment order.

Maersk India filed its objections before Dispute Resolution Panel ("DRP") stating that the assessee was a low-end back office service provider being a captive unit working in a zero risk zone and hence should not be categorized as a KPO and high margin comparables selected by the TPO should be dropped. The DRP maintained the high margin comparables selected by TPO on the premise that both high and low margin companies reflect industry profitability and dispensing off super-profit making companies symbolizes addressing only one end of the spectrum and that is not correct. The DRP further disapproved the segmental bifurcation of services by the assessee as IT and ITeS. DRP directed the TPO to benchmark the international transactions with ten final comparables comprising of five comparables selected by the assessee and TPO each. The Panel did not allow relief on risk adjustment.

PARUL MITTAL

CA

Introduction

1. The Indian IT/ ITeS industry has witnessed exceptional growth in the last decade and has been instrumental in registering a multi-fold increase in foreign exchange earnings for the country. In addition to fuelling India's economy, this industry is also positively influencing the lives of its people through contributing in employment generation and augmenting standards of living. The industry has helped India transform from a rural and agriculture-based economy to a knowledge based economy.

As per a recent NASSCOM report, the Indian IT-BPO industry's aggregate revenues have crossed the USD 100 billion mark with exports of USD 69 billion in year 2012. Within Software and services exports, IT services accounts for 58 per cent and BPO is nearly 23 per cent, Engineering and R&D ('ER&D') and Software Products account for 19 per cent.

The mitochondria of Indian IT sector can be broadly divided into two segments on the basis of nature of services performed. On one hand, there are Indian IT Companies like Wipro, Infosys, HCL, etc., who have established their footprint on the global scale by establishing offshore software product development centres ('OSPD'). India's OSPD market has experienced double digit growth over the past five years. On the other hand, there are inbound investments by various foreign multi-national IT Companies like Microsoft, IBM, Genpact, Capgemini etc. where predominantly foreign IT majors outsource their research, software development and testing to captive Indian subsidiaries or through Global In-house centres ('GIC').

Various steps involved in software development projects

2. A software development project typically entails various steps starting from conception of the desired software, research and application development, software design, writing and maintaining source code, prototyping, modification, re-engineering, maintenance and other activities.

Ideally, a full-fledged software company should undertake all the phases involved in software development. However, such is not the case always. Mostly, software companies outsource certain parts of their software development functions to their offshore subsidiaries stationed in nations with a rich knowledge base, anticipating cost-effectiveness in operations due to low human resource cost. In such type of arrangements, generally the conceptualization and quality assessment aspects are taken care of by the parent software company only, whereas the captive subsidiaries are only involved in functional research and development activities. Such captive subsidiaries are named as 'contract R&D centres' due to the limited nature of work handled by them. Usually, the major part of risk-taking work in terms of business development, bidding, sales and marketing is done by the parent company in such cases, thereby ensuring consistent work flow to their captive R&D centres. The contract R&D centres in return undertake to complete the work assigned to them as per the quality specifications. This arrangement can be compared to the traditional outsourcing model where the work execution is done by the sub-contracted company (in this case a captive subsidiary) to the satisfaction of the customer (in this case the parent company).

The Transfer Pricing Controversy

3. Transfer Pricing ('TP') is one of the major concerns for IT companies today. There are widespread TP adjustments and additions in many cases. Many issues that are being faced by IT sector today pertain to choice of comparables where divergence of opinion occurs between the taxpayer and the revenue on the inclusion of companies as comparables, matter relating to choice of Most Appropriate Method ('MAM'), issues surrounding the quantitative and qualitative filters, use of multiple year's data, disagreement on crediting the benefit of working capital adjustment, revenue denying the benefit of +/-5 per cent range, etc.

From several TP issues faced by the Indian IT sector today, one major TP issue relates to the margins charged by IT companies. The tax authorities are consistently proposing margin of 20-27 per cent for the IT segment, while the taxpayer attributes a downward trend in the margins, experienced within 12-15 per cent. The comparables selected by the tax authorities are big companies like Wipro, HCL. These are independent business enterprises taking extensive risks and infusing large asset base in their business. The margins computed by the tax authorities swell the moment such comparables are added to the basket of identified comparable companies. On the other hand, in case of captive research centres, major business development functions, risks and assets associated with the software development operations are borne by foreign parent companies, the price paid by them ought to be lower in comparison to cases where both the associated enterprises operate on a principal-to-principal basis.

To address the issues faced by the IT sector companies, a committee chaired by N Rangachary, former Chairman, CBDT was formed last year. The Committee penned out its suggestions in September last year, which were not made public. Out of several suggestions made by the Rangachary Committee, one of the key recommendations has been a 20 per cent safe harbour rate for IT/ ITeS sector. Further, the Committee is understood to be favouring the cost plus method over profit-split method.

The Tribunal held that the financial data of Maple e-solutions was not available for the full financial year but was available only for four months during the financial year 2004-05. It was held that the part period data could not be considered as a comparable to determine the arm's length price.

EMPLOYEES COST 11. In Electronics Data Processing (I) (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [IT Appeal No. 420/Hyd/07] the Tribunal held that there was no dispute to the fact that the employees cost to the total turnover of the selected company worked out to be 1.42% as against the industry's average of 30-40% and the assessee's employees cost to turnover percentage was 43%. This fact implied that the selected company had outsourced major portion of its work to third party vendors. Therefore, the company could not be treated as a comparable.

In Google India (P.) Ltd. (supra)it was held that any company with employee cost less than 25% could not be compared with an ITES company – in this case Vishal IT Limited had been adopted by the TPO. This company outsourced its call centre work and, therefore, the employees cost was less than 25% as was the common practice among other ITES. When company had outsourced its ITES, it could not be said that its business results would be comparable to any other ITES provider rendering the services entirely on its own. In such circumstances the net margins of the two comparables could not be on the same basis.

BUSINESS MODEL

12. In Capital IQ Infrastructure Systems (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT (International Taxation) [2013] 57 SOT 14/ 32 taxmann.com 21 (Hyd. – Trib.) the Tribunal found that Dispute Resolution Panel, in the proceedings for the assessment year 2008-09 in the assessee's own case, after taking note of the composition of the vendor payments of Coral Hub for the last three years and the fact that it also commenced a new line of business of printing on demand, wherein it printed upon clients request, in view of the major difference in functionality and the business model the Panel was of the view that 'Coral Hub' was not a suitable comparable to the taxpayer and, hence, it needed to be dropped from the final list of comparables.

SUPER PROFIT COMPANIES

13. In Google India (P.) Ltd. (supra)it was held that the super profit margin companies were to be excluded from the list of comparables for the purposes of transfer pricing study – in this case two companies showed profit of more than 100% as compared to other companies taken by the TPO.

EXTRAORDINARY EVENTS

14. In Google India (P.) Ltd. (supra)it was held that in respect of two companies Datamatics Financial Services and Allsec Technologies Limited, the Tribunal found that merely because there were extraordinary events during the financial year without demonstrating as to how these extraordinary events had influenced the profit margin of the companies they could not be excluded from the list of comparables, but the adjustments for such extraordinary events had to be made to the profits of the companies to bring them on par with the assessee before comparing them with the assessee.

ARITHMETIC MEAN

15. First proviso to section 92C(2) provides that where more than one price is determined by the most appropriate method, the arm's length price shall be taken to be the arithmetical mean of such prices.

In Simphony Marketing Solutions India (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2013] 38 taxmann.com 55 (Bang. – Trib.)the assessee had selected nine comparables identified by it at arithmetical mean of 14.84% in relation to the disclosed margins of 14.91%, the difference being within the tolerance limit of 5%. The TPO added 18 more comparables to the two accepted by him. The TPO worked out the arithmetical mean at 22.28% after making an adjustment to the benchmark for working capital. If nine comparables which according to the assessee were wrongly included were excluded, it would work out to be an arithmetical mean of 7.97% only as against 14.91% disclosed by the assessee, so that there could have been no addition. The DRP affirmed the addition of TPO. The Tribunal found that out of 20 companies chosen by the TPO as comparables only 11 companies were found to be comparables and their arithmetic mean was only 7.97%. The profit margin cost of the assessee was 14.91% which was made higher than the arithmetic mean of comparable companies chosen by the TPO after the exclusion of some of the comparable companies. The reasons for exclusions of 9 companies were on the following grounds:

During the previous year, there were extraordinary events that took place which warranted exclusion as a comparable;

The comparable company performed knowledge process outsourcing and the assessee was doing business process outsourcing;

The comparable company outsourced most of the work and the assessee was carrying out work by itself;

risk, working capital etc., there is a disproportionate variation between the margins of the captive entities and that of the comparables. This approach of the revenue has resulted in transfer pricing adjustments of thousands of crores in the captive IT/ITeS industry. As an illustration, the arithmetical mean Net Cost Plus Markup ('NCP') of the comparables adopted during Transfer Pricing Assessments have been as follows:

Table 2: Mean NCP of comparables selected by the revenue authorities6 It is evident from Table 1 that the arm's length markups on cost determined by the revenue authorities for the captive IT and ITeS service providers have been in the range of 20% to 30%, which is in stark contrast to the much lower markups earned historically by GICs in India. This has been the moot cause for the significant high adjustments and continuous transfer pricing disputes and protracted litigation in the captive IT/ITeS space.

Another contention of the Indian revenue authorities in relation to captive development centers in India is that the cost savings associated with operating in a low cost jurisdiction like India (commonly referred to as 'location savings') should be considered while carrying out comparability analysis. This is also emphasized in the United Nations Practice Manual on Transfer Pricing for Developing Countries (also referred to as the 'UN Practice Manual'). Further, the Location Specific Advantages ('LSAs') derived by MNEs in addition to the location savings are further identified in the UN Practice Manual as below:

Highly specialized skilled manpower and knowledge

Access and proximity to growing local/regional market

Large customer base with increased spending capacity

Superior information network

Superior distribution network

Incentives

Market premium

The Indian Transfer Pricing administration believes it is possible to use the profit split method to determine arm's length allocation of location savings and rents in cases where comparable uncontrolled transactions are not available.

India being a low cost jurisdiction attracts the attention of a lot of MNE groups who intend to exploit the advantages of location savings and LSAs. As a result it may well be argued that the any tangible benefit accruing to such MNE groups is not exclusive and hence does not provide any durable competitive advantage. Accordingly, it becomes very difficult to quantify and allocate any location specific benefits between AEs.

In fact the profit split method is also advocated by the Indian revenue authorities in case of development centers engaged in significant R&D activities. In this regard, it is pertinent to note the CBDT had issued Circular 2/2013 dated 26 March 2013 promoting the use of profit split method for benchmarking of R&D activities by development centers in India. The said circular was subsequently withdrawn upon representations from the industry about possible misinterpretation of the said circular. However, the CBDT issued Circular 6/2013 dated 29 June 2013 providing guidelines to identify R&D service providers with insignificant risk. Although the circular aims to provide clarity in analyzing the functions of captive development centers in India and thereby the selection of the most appropriate method for benchmarking, it may well be argued that the same is still amenable to misinterpretation giving rise to transfer pricing disputes.

Transfer Pricing litigation in the captive IT/ITeS space

Following are the broad areas of litigation that have emerged over the years consequent to the aggressive approach adopted by the revenue:

1. Functional comparability

As per Para 1.33 of the OECD Guidelines, application of the arm's length principle is generally based on a comparison of the conditions in a controlled transaction with conditions in transactions between independent enterprises. For such comparison to be appropriate, the economically relevant characteristics of the situations being compared must be sufficiently comparable. The concept of comparability has been further elucidated by stating that, to be comparable means that none of the differences (if any) between the situations being compared could materially affect the condition being examined in the methodology (e.g. price or margin), or that reasonably accurate adjustments can be made to eliminate the effect of any such differences.

Para 1.36 lays down the factors that may be considered when determining comparability between controlled and uncontrolled transactions and enterprises. These factors are listed as below:

Characteristics of the property or services transferred,

Functions performed by the parties (taking into account assets used and risks assumed),

Contractual terms,

Economic circumstances of the parties, and

Business strategies pursued by the parties

The above referred principles have also been reiterated in the UN Practice Manual.

The principles of comparability under the Indian Income Tax law also largely mirror the above referred principles laid down in the OECD Guidelines. The same are listed under Rule 10B(2) and Rule 10B(3) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 ('Rules').

The principles of comparability enshrined in the OECD Guidelines as well as the Indian Income Tax law, were relied upon by the Delhi High Court in the case of CIT v. Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. 2. KPO VS. BPO CONTROVERSY – AN ANALYSIS

In both the business formats, it is not a simple case of "K" replacing the "B". BPO usually deals with performing business activities like customer care, finance, HR, voice and data entry functions. The extent of work force required is more process driven and elementary. Generally, the motivation of setting up of BPO operations is substantial cost savings. On the other hand, KPO, being a subset of BPO, involves the outsourcing of core specialized and knowledge based services which may or may not result in cost savings but surely adds value to parent company's endeavours. Services outsourced to KPO are related to research and development, equity and financial analysis, legal services, biotechnology, animation and design and other services to likes of dedicated business solutions. KPO employs qualified professionals having specific industry expertise.

The Hon'ble Special Bench has pronounced that the process followed to identify potential comparables is one of the most critical aspects of the comparability analysis and it should be transparent, systematic and verifiable. Potential comparables in ITeS sector can be identified through applying "broad functionality test" by analyzing the taxpayer's circumstances largely. Further bifurcation of IT enabled services may be done to establish relatively equal degree of comparability. The line of differentiation between KPO and BPO is very thin since KPOs are an upward extension of BPO industry in the value chain. Since KPO is an evolution of BPO, there is a likely-hood where in the process of such evolution, there are entities offering a mix of overlapping services which are difficult to classify as either BPO or KPO, going by their functional profile.

The Special Bench held that IT Enables Services cannot be further bifurcated or classified as BPO and KPO services for comparability purposes in wake of difficulty in classifying services strictly either as low end BPO services or high end KPO services. The Bench advocated a two step process to benchmark transactions in the ITeS sector :-

Identifying potential comparables through conducting a broad functional analysis at ITeS level; and

Comparing the functional profile of tested party with principal functions performed by selected entities, ensuring equal comparability. Such functional filtration process may ensure that the uncontrolled transactions having lesser degree of comparability would get eliminated.

Hence, in essence, the Bench iterated that the selection of final comparables shall depend on facts and circumstances of each case on the basis of functional profile of the tested party.

In light of above analysis, Maersk India is held to be a captive contract service provider mainly rendering back office support services and other incidental services involving some degree of special knowledge and expertise. Hence, Mold-Tek Technologies and eClerx Services were dropped as comparables on the premise that both companies were engaged in providing high-end services involving specialized knowledge and domain expertise.

3. WHETHER DEFINITIONS IN SAFE HARBOUR RULES CAN BE SANCTIONED IN ALL CASES

One of the contentions put up by the taxpayer for justifying the differentiation between KPO and BPO is the definition of "Information technology enables services" cited in the Final Safe Harbour Rules ("SHR" or "the Rules") released issued by Ministry of Finance on September 18, 2013. The aforesaid definition is an exclusive one that identifies many low-end outsourcing services viz. payroll, revenue accounting, call centre services. "Knowledge process outsourcing services" are separately defined in the aforesaid Rules as outsourcing services provided mainly with the assistance or use of information technology requiring application of knowledge and advanced analytical and technical skill. Hence, the assessee submitted that specific articulation by the CBDT of both BPO and KPO in the SHR demonstrates the differences between the two business layouts.

The Revenue challenged the assessee's reference to the SHR on the ground that the aforesaid rules were released in September 2013 and cannot be applied retrospectively to a case pertaining to AY 2008-09. Besides, the Revenue countered the assessee's reliance on definitions provided in SHR by submitting that the assessee in this case has not exercised the safe harbour option and hence cannot draw an inference from it. However, the Special Bench did not place any strictures on such reliance by non-safe harbour pickers.

Despite the need for an appropriate risk adjustment, typically it is observed that the field officers disallowed such adjustments to taxpayers, citing reasons of the "single customer risk" borne by the captive service providers, surpassing various other risks that the captive does not bear e.g. success/failure for the activities such entities perform. Although the need for a risk adjustment has been disregarded at the lower echelons of power, it is encouraging to note that the Tribunals in various instances have taken a contrary view on this matter. In the case of Intellinet Technologies6, the Bangalore Tribunal has observed the need for providing a risk adjustment. The Tribunal in the said ruling has taken cognizance of the principles of economic adjustments and emphasised the need to carry out risk adjustments, with a specific reference to the point that the single customer risk borne by the captive service providers is only an "anticipated risk". This apart, the ruling has remained silent on the methodology and approach to be adopted for undertaking a risk based adjustment.

In fact, it is observed that in several other decisions, although the Tribunals have adjudicated the need for carrying out a risk adjustment, there continues to remain a lack of clarity on the methodology to be adopted for undertaking the same. One may not fault the Tribunals for not setting an approach to such risk adjustment, since the topic itself is complex and desirous of a separate analysis. Many a company have attempted to demonstrate the basis of arriving at a risk based adjustment, however, the final word on it still remains elusive.

Having said that there are contrary views doing the rounds, specifically in the case of GE India Technology Centre7, wherein the Tribunal has placed the onus on the taxpayer to prove that the risk can be remotely controlled by the overseas parent. Further, the observations of the Bangalore Tribunal in the instance case are in line with the comments of the Indian tax administrators in the recent India chapter as part of the UN Manual. While the UN Manual appreciates that "risk" is an important element in the comparability analysis, it does not treat the risk bearing capacity of an enterprise as an independent element, but similar to the functions performed and assets deployed. Additionally, the UN Manual also mentions that the conduct of the parties should provide the key to determine whether the actual allocation of risk conforms to such contractual risk allocation. A mere agreement citing the contractual arrangement, along with hard evidences (like demonstrating the difference in risks profiling in various situations) may help the tested party to fortify their stand for a risk-based adjustment.

Outliers and the risk dimension

To reiterate, there do exist certain fundamental principles, where the Indian TP legislation deviate from the globally accepted best practices. The adoption of the arithmetical mean as a measure of central tendency in the Indian context as against the inter-quartile range or the median, which are the internationally accepted measures of central tendency, as they tend to eliminate outliers, and are better representatives of the industry averages is one such major exception. This coupled with the use of single year data for the purpose of comparability analysis, daunts taxpayers in the IT/ITeS sector and is the prime reason for the increasing disputes, particularly in this sector. The law, through a proviso, does provide for expanding the base of comparable data, going back up to two further years back from the year of the transaction, thereby allowing for a three-year comparability analysis. Though overseas approaches suggest a 5-year period for any comparability analysis, one may accept a 3-year period specifically for developing countries like India, which has been witnessing contrasting growth year-on-year. Incidentally, the IT/ITeS sectors have been through such tumultuous times over the past decade. However, from the field officers' perspective and indeed the Tribunals, the approach has been to rely on the so-called "contemporaneous data", a phase contained in the legislation but often misused for annual audits. This, along with the concept of mean, has meant that expected mark-up drives comparability selection, rather than the reverse.

The adoption of the arithmetical mean as the arm's length price, hitherto with a limited tolerance band, has its inherent limitations and poses its own set of challenges. Unlike the median and the inter-quartile range, the arithmetical mean tends to be influenced by extreme values and the results are therefore skewed towards either very high/loss making companies. It is for this reason that there exist huge variations in the profitability of comparables arrived at by the Indian Revenue authorities during the course of the audit process, vis-à-vis the ex-post comparability analysis performed by the taxpayer to defend their position. Given that the results so arrived at are not representative of the normal industry averages, consisting varied types of entities in varied stages of growth, there definitely exists an immediate need to provide taxpayers with certain leeway in the form of a risk based adjustment.

The Information Technology ("IT")/ Business Process Outsourcing ("BPO") sector in India has experienced spectacular growth over the past decade and half. The Indian success story in the global outsourcing industry has become a leading example for other developing economies. While this growth model has been discussed from a macro level widely, it is important to study the same from a micro level to understand and evaluate the challenges and advantages faced by the various players who have been a catalyst to this chronicle. This article aims to appraise the Indian IT sector from a transfer pricing perspective.

The Indian IT industry has several players, each of whom faces unique transfer pricing challenges. This article provides an overview of the Indian IT/BPO outsourcing industry, the players and the transfer pricing framework that they operate in.

The Indian IT landscape can be broadly classified based on the nature of players operating in the industry. On one end of the spectrum, there are Indian IT giants like Wipro, Infosys, HCL etc. who represent Indian IT outbound investment in the global IT industry. These are predominantly Indian multinationals that have subsidiaries and branch offices across the globe. On the other end of the spectrum there are Global In-House centers (GIC) or 'captive services providers' who operate as delivery centers for foreign IT Multinationals Corporation ("MNCs") and represent the inbound investment in the Indian IT sector.

The GIC1 segment which till 2003, constituted a very small part of the IT/BPO industry has witnessed spectacular growth over the past few years. Currently the segment contributes to 22% of India's IT-BPO revenue and accounts for almost 21% of the industry's employment. Based on the latest available data, this segment has grown at a CAGR of 22% between 2003 -2010. In the fiscal year 2009-10, the Indian GICs contributed to almost 1% of the national GDP†. Spanning across all the major cities of India the segment provides direct and indirect employment to about 1.8 million people2.

The GIC model has played an important role in the IT/BPO outsourcing industry globally. This model originated in the 80s and 90s, when several big MNCs realized they could substantially lower their operating cost by opening delivery centers in low cost locations like India. The GIC model has been a global success for the IT Industry. Not only has it helped parent MNCs to lower their operational cost, it has boosted the economies of the offshoring locations as well. As per a Nasscom –Everest Report, presently there are about 3000 GICs operating around the globe in various countries.

The Indian IT Industry watch-dog, Nasscom reports that there are presently about 750 IT/BPO MNCs in India and they operate across almost all the verticals like Aerospace & Defence, Automotive, BFSI, Bio-Technology, Chemicals, Computer Hardware, Education, Electronic/Electrical Equipment, Energy, Healthcare, Industrial, Semiconductors, Software/Internet, and Telecommunications, etc. Engineering, Research and Development (ER&D) and Software Product Development companies form the largest segment within the Indian captive industry. This particular segment has especially witnessed a tremendous growth in MNCs opening their ER&D delivery centers in India over the past couple of years. Geography-wise, North America and Europe comprise 90 per cent of this segment in India.

Although India still remains one of the preferred GIC locations in the world, MNCs are increasingly looking towards other low cost destinations like the Philippines, East Asia, Eastern Europe Latin America and even Africa for opening new delivery centers to further their cost arbitrage benefit. Thus, while it is easy to bask in the glory of the success story that India has paved in the realm of the IT Industry, it is crucial to watch out for competition in other emerging IT capabilities in Asia, South America and other parts of the globe. Countries like Philippines, Cost Rica, Russian Federation, Ukraine, Argentina, Sri Lanka etc. have witnessed remarkable growth in IT exports in their economy in the recent past. Being at the nascent stage of the IT Industry, the volume of exports by these economies has been low. But the growth rates experienced by them have been well above the average growth rates of large exporters like the European Union, India and the United States. Between 2005 to 20113 the Philippines IT exports has grown at 69%, Ukraine witnessed a growth of 59% in IT service exports, followed by Argentina and Costa Rica at 37% and 35% respectively.

Bottleneck in TP

In a transfer pricing matter more often than not we get to read an observation or a remark by the Courts and Tribunal/DRP that 'we are unable to treat this company fit for comparability analysis for determining the arm's length price for the assessee in the absence of segmental details'. Also benches of the Tribunal in more than one instance have held that 'segmental results does not give a true picture and may not be always be correct and precise because it is almost impossible to distribute certain common expenses. The Delhi bench of the ITAT in DHL Express (India) (P.) Ltd v. Asstt CIT (2012) 12 ITR (Trib) 658 held that the assessee's objection for rejecting the Transport Corporation of India as comparable is also devoid of any merits, because when pro per comparable companies are available, there is no requirement for making comparison with segmental results which does not give a true picture. Later it also remarked that it is a known fact that segmental results may not be always correct and precise because it is almost impossible to distribute certain common expenses.

However, till date there is no law or section that bars a comparable being chosen on segmental results basis. Transfer pricing is a subjective phenomenon where the assessee has all the right to substantiate its price on whatever material is available with him which may even be in the form of segmental results of an enterprise. Rule 10D proviso says it all on such right given to the assessee. The words 'on the basis of material available with him' in the proviso are sheer pointer to this fact. Hence the view held by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal to hold that segmental results are untrue and unreliable is not in accordance with the law.

Inclusion or exclusion of a comparable make a vital difference in the determination of arms length price because of which a transfer pricing study could actually fail.

It is therefore important that the proviso to rule 10D must also be read as sufficient a provision that enables production of segmental results as a material relevant in the exercise of determination of arm's length price.

It is an irony that on one hand we complain that segmental results are not available and right on the other side we hold stand that the segmental results are not true. These disconnects have to go somehow from the judicial interface.

TP Criteria

In the prime most it is desirable to have the segmental details for revenue/sales of varieties of product and service dealt by an enterprise. At the same time the financials must also provide for segmental details of operating income of respective variety of product and services. These two are essentials for assessing the comparability for carrying out study and determination of arms length price with a testing party. Accounting Standard 17 further states that an enterprise should comply with the requirements of this Standard fully and not selectively. However often we find that there is unallocated sums that are adjusted against the total income for one reason or the other. This kind of reporting goes adverse to the accounting standard and must also be reported as a qualification by the auditor in their report.

Now the proviso to rule 10D of the Income tax Rules, 1962 require upon an assessee to substantiate on the basis of material available with him that the income arising from international transactions entered into by him has been computed in accordance with section 92. One is expected to maintain prescribed documents for this purpose if the value of international transactions exceeds Rs. 1 crore. To substantiate one's price one is required to have matching results of operation of a comparable company. Often there is a difficulty to make such an assessment in the absence of similar comparable hence one employ software with various kind of filters to arrive at one lot of comparables. And out of these some fails for one reason or the other as we go up in the ladder before dispute resolution process, Tribunal and Courts.

If we have segmental accounting in its proper form and substance the entire exercise of transfer pricing could be made more simpler and accurate.
