2.8-7 Will there be a disallowance under section 44DA?

Section 44DA deals with the taxability of royalties and fees for technical services connected to the PE in India. The first proviso to section 44DA disallows the deduction in respect of the following:

(a)

Any expenditure or allowance that is not wholly or exclusively incurred for the business of such permanent establishment or fixed place of profession in India; or

(b) Amount paid by the permanent establishment to its head office or to any of its other offices. However, deduction shall be allowed where such payment is made by way of reimbursement of expenses.

As the proviso to section 44BBD(2) excludes the applicability of section 44DA, the above expenditure should not be disallowed if the royalty and FTS connected to the PE in India are taxable on a presumptive basis under section 44BBD.

2.8-8 Would other disallowance provisions apply?

Section 44BBD(1) begins with a non-obstante clause that "Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in sections 28 to 43A...". Section 44B(1) contains an identical non-obstante clause, which the CBDT has explained in its Circular No. 169, dated 23-6-1975, as follows:

38. It should be noted that the new section 44B overrides the provisions of sections 28 to 43A only and, accordingly other provisions (including those relating to aggregation of income and set off or carry forward and set off of losses) will continue to apply in the case of non-residents deriving profits from shipping business . In this connection, it may be mentioned that unabsorbed depreciation allowance is carried forward under section 32(2) and the unabsorbed depreciation allowance of earlier years is treated as part of the depreciation allowance admissible in the relevant previous year. Since the provisions of section 32 are specifically overridden by the new section 44B, the unabsorbed depreciation for earlier years will not be allowed in determining the profits and gains for the assessment year 1976-77 and subsequent years. Losses incurred in earlier years, other than the losses due to depreciation will, however, be allowed to be set off against the profits for the assessment year 1976-77 and subsequent years subject to the fulfilment of the existing conditions in this behalf.

The non-obstante clause overriding sections 28 to 43A will mean that 25% presumptive profit under section 44BBD will be treated as having been arrived at after making disallowances referred to in section 37(2B), section 40, section 40A and the Explanations below section 37(1) of the Act. Section 44BBD is not expressed to override Section 43B by the non-obstante clause in section 44BBC(1). Therefore, disallowances under Section 43B52, including Clause (h) of Section 43B (disallowance for outstandings to Micro and Small Enterprises as at balance sheet date not paid within due date under MSMED ACT), shall apply to assessees covered under the presumptive tax scheme under section 43BBD.

2.8-9 Will DTAA override section 44BBD53?

The CBDT54 clarified that the correct legal position is that where a specific provision is made in the DTAA, that provision will prevail over the general provisions contained in the ITA. Accordingly, the Circular states that income and tax shall be computed by following the DTAA provisions irrespective of the ITA provision.

The Gujarat High Court55 has held that the provisions of the DTAA override the specific provisions of the ITA. Various juridical fora have held the same view, which was subsequently upheld by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Azadi Bachao Andolan [2003] 132 Taxman 373 (SC).

The Hon'ble SC has held:

'If it was not the intention of the legislature to make a departure from the general principle of chargeability to tax under section 4 and the general principle of ascertainment of total income under section 5 of the Act, then there was no purpose in making those sections "subject to the provisions" of the Act. The very object of grafting the said two sections with the said clause is to enable the Central Government to issue a notification under section 90 towards implementation of the terms of the DTAs which would automatically override the provisions of the Income-tax Act in the matter of ascertainment of chargeability to income tax and ascertainment of total income, to the extent of inconsistency with the terms of the DTAC.'

If the Indian data centre's role is limited to managing data centre infrastructure and is not involved in concluding contracts or securing orders in India for the foreign company's services to overseas users, then the DAPE risk may not arise. Section 9(6)(b) defines 'royalty' to include consideration for the use or right to use any industrial, commercial or scientific equipment. The classification of data centre services as 'royalty' has been a subject of judicial scrutiny. Indian courts, such as the Mumbai ITAT in Rackspace US, Inc. v. DCIT [2021] 124 taxmann.com 92, have held that income from cloud hosting and ancillary services was neither royalty nor Fees for Technical Services (FTS). The Tribunal observed that the agreement was for providing hosting services simpliciter, not for the use or leasing of equipment, as customers did not have physical control or possession over the servers. If the foreign company retains control and operational responsibility for the data centre infrastructure and merely provides a service to overseas users, the income is unlikely to be classified as royalty. Furthermore, in case the users are overseas, the requirement that the royalty be for the use of a right/property in a business/income source in India would generally not be met.

The use of a data centre by a foreign company providing services to overseas or Indian users may not give rise to royalty income under a DTAA, given the specific interpretation of 'royalty' in these treaties and consistent judicial precedents. The definition of 'royalty' in most DTAAs entered into by India is typically narrower than the broad definition provided under section 9(6)(b) of the ITA 2025. DTAAs often require a more direct nexus to the use or right to use specific intellectual property or equipment, or the transfer of technical know-how. For payments to be classified as royalty for the 'use or right to use industrial, commercial or scientific equipment' under a DTAA, judicial pronouncements39 consistently emphasise that the payer (user) must have physical control or possession over the equipment.

Therefore, if the data centre services involve providing access to software, platforms, or infrastructure without transferring the underlying intellectual property rights or granting users control over or possession of the equipment, the income is unlikely to be characterised as royalty under the DTAA. It would typically be considered business profits, taxable only if a Permanent Establishment (PE) exists in India.

8.7-11d Computation of taxable income - The taxable income arising to the foreign company, for which the exemption under this entry is not available, will depend on whether the foreign company has a PE in India.

Business income connected to PE in India

If the foreign company has a PE in India and the business income earned in India is connected to that PE, the tax liability shall be computed in accordance with the ITA.

Business income not connected to PE in India

If the foreign company does not have a PE in India, its business income earned in India shall not be taxable in India.

8.7-12 Transaction with associated enterprises

Where an Indian entity provides data centre services to its associated enterprise (a foreign company), it may opt for the safe harbour framework under the transfer pricing provisions. If the Indian entity earns an operating profit margin of at least 15% of operating expenses from such international transactions, the transaction price will be deemed to be at arm's length, and no transfer pricing adjustment will be required. [see Para 12.2-2b]

There are five parties in the transaction relating to the data centre: SCloud Pte. Ltd. (a Singapore-based cloud management platform), DC Ltd. (an Indian data centre), RS India Ltd. (an Indian reseller), OTT Pvt. Ltd. (the Indian end user) and OS Inc. (the Singapore-based end user).

The details of the transaction between the parties are as follows:

DC enters into an agreement with SCloud to provide 50 servers, 10TB storage, power, cooling, and facility services for Rs. 7,00,000 per month. DC owns and operates all physical equipment, while SCloud has only API access to manage virtual resources and no ownership or physical control.

SCloud enters into a reseller agreement with RS, offering managed cloud services (including the DC infrastructure, SCloud proprietary management platform, orchestration software, 24/7 monitoring, technical support, and analytics) for Rs. 13,50,000 per month.

SCloud enters into a cloud service agreement with OS, under which OS offers managed cloud services for USD 50,000 per month.

The supplier of backend services located in India arranges or facilitates the supply of goods or services or both by the client located abroad to the customers of client. back office operations;

advertised product or service outside India. In such a case, both the buyer and the seller are non-residents; yet on a literal reading, if the advertisement has been accessed through IP address located in India, its income may be covered by the Explanation.

(f)

Services:

The term 'services' would cover all types of services whether technical, consultancy, managerial, or otherwise. Section 9(1) creates a legal fiction under which certain incomes are deemed to accrue or arise in India. Section 9(2) (corresponding to Section 9(1)(i) of the ITA 1961) provides a set of circumstances in which income accruing or arising, directly or indirectly, through or from any nexus with India is taxable in India. Clause (c) of section 9(2) provides that the income accruing or arising through or from any business connection in India shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India. 'Business Connection' has not been defined explicitly in the Income-tax Act. However, the inclusive meaning of the term 'business connection' has been provided in section 9(9), which covers the following:

(a)

Any business carried out in India, in the case of which all or part of the operation is carried out in India.

(b)

Significant Economic Presence in India.

In this scenario, A foreign company selling data centre services, sourced from an Indian data centre that fulfils the conditions specified in Schedule IV: Table Sl. No. 13C, to overseas clients, may not create a business connection in India. This is because the entire infrastructure and resources of the data centre are owned and operated by the Indian data centre provider, and the foreign company merely receives services from it. Accordingly, the foreign company cannot be regarded as carrying on any business operations in India on its own.

Further, where such services are sold only to overseas clients, the conditions for Significant Economic Presence (SEP) would not be triggered, as the primary requirement for transactions with users in India is not satisfied. However, if the services are provided to users in India, a business connection may arise in India on account of SEP.

8.7-11b Income attributable to Permanent Establishment - Most DTAAs define a 'Permanent Establishment' (PE) as a threshold for taxing business profits of a non-resident in the source country (India). One must evaluate the following types of PE relevant to data centres:

Fixed Place PE

A 'permanent establishment' typically means a fixed place of business through which the business of an enterprise is wholly or partly carried on. This includes a place of management, a branch, an office, a factory, a workshop, etc. A data centre, being a physical location with servers and related equipment, could be considered a 'fixed place of business'. The OECD Commentary on Article 5 clarifies that a server, as a piece of equipment having a physical location, may constitute a 'fixed place of business' of the enterprise that operates it. If the foreign company has significant control and disposal over the servers in the Indian data centre, and these servers perform core income-generating activities, it is likely to constitute a fixed place PE.

Dependent Agent PE (DAPE)

A Dependent Agent PE (DAPE) can arise if a person (agent) acts on behalf of a non-resident enterprise and is not an independent agent. A PE can be deemed if the agent habitually exercises authority to conclude contracts on behalf of the enterprise, or habitually secures orders wholly or principally for the enterprise. A DAPE is generally not constituted if the agent is an 'independent agent' acting in the ordinary course of its business. An agent is considered independent if it is legally and economically independent of the foreign enterprise and acts at arm's length. If the agent acts exclusively or almost exclusively for the foreign enterprise, it may not be considered an independent agent. If the Indian data centre's role is limited to managing data centre infrastructure and is not involved in concluding contracts or securing orders in India for the foreign company's services to overseas users, then the DAPE risk may not arise. However, if the Indian entity facilitates the foreign company's contracts with overseas or Indian users in any significant way from India, it may result in a DAPE.

Fixed Place PE

A 'permanent establishment' typically means a fixed place of business through which the business of an enterprise is wholly or partly carried on. This includes a place of management, a branch, an office, a factory, a workshop, etc. A data centre, being a physical location with servers and related equipment, could be considered a 'fixed place of business'. The OECD Commentary on Article 5 clarifies that a server, as a piece of equipment having a physical location, may constitute a 'fixed place of business' of the enterprise that operates it. If the foreign company has significant control and disposal over the servers in the Indian data centre, and these servers perform core income-generating activities, it is likely to constitute a fixed place PE.

Dependent Agent PE (DAPE)

A Dependent Agent PE (DAPE) can arise if a person (agent) acts on behalf of a non-resident enterprise and is not an independent agent. A PE can be deemed if the agent habitually exercises authority to conclude contracts on behalf of the enterprise, or habitually secures orders wholly or principally for the enterprise. A DAPE is generally not constituted if the agent is an 'independent agent' acting in the ordinary course of its business. An agent is considered independent if it is legally and economically independent of the foreign enterprise and acts at arm's length. If the agent acts exclusively or almost exclusively for the foreign enterprise, it may not be considered an independent agent. If the Indian data centre's role is limited to managing data centre infrastructure and is not involved in concluding contracts or securing orders in India for the foreign company's services to overseas users, then the DAPE risk may not arise. However, if the Indian entity facilitates the foreign company's contracts with overseas or Indian users in any significant way from India, it may result in a DAPE.

8.7-7a Data Centre Services - Note 3(b) of Table in Schedule IV specifies the meaning of data centre services. The definition mentions rendering of services "through the use of" which suggests the servers and computers should be operated by the data centre.

(c)

The foreign company does not own or operate any of the resources of the data centre [see Para 8.7-8].

To claim the exemption, the foreign company should procure data centre services that cover everything from power equipment and cooling systems to servers, computers, storage systems, operating systems, security solutions, network and associated software platforms, and other equipment from the specified data centre. 12.2-5 Separate safe harbour procedures are prescribed for IT and non-IT service transactions.

Rule 10TE of IT Rules 1962 prescribes the mechanism for exercising the safe harbour option in respect of all eligible international transactions covering IT services (software development, ITeS, KPO), intra-group loans, corporate guarantees, contract R&D (software and pharma), and auto component transactions. This rule did not distinguish between IT and non-IT transactions and provided a single unified procedure across all eligible categories.

The IT Rules 2026 contain two rules providing the distinct procedures to apply for the safe harbour:

Rule 90 for non-IT transactions [see Para 12.2-5a]

Rule 91 for IT services [see Para 12.2-5b]

12.2-5a Safe harbour for transactions other than provision of information technology services [Rule 90] - Rule 90 of the IT Rules 2026 governs safe harbour for eligible international transactions other than the provision of information technology services. This category encompasses intra-group loans, corporate guarantees, contract R&D services, receipt of low-value-adding intra-group services, and outbound manufacturing/trading transactions.

The eligible assessee must file Form No. 49 [Form 3CEFA in IT Rules 1962] to the Assessing Officer on or before the due date for filing the return of income. The return must be filed before or on the date Form No. 49 is filed. The limitation period is similar to that provided in Rule 10TE.

Unlike Rule 10TE of IT Rules 1962, which allowed the specification of a multi-year period, Rule 90 of IT Rules 2026 is explicitly a single tax-year mechanism. The option must be exercised each year afresh. This represents a structural change for non-IT assessees who previously could make a multi-year election under Form 3CEFA.

It is pertinent to note that the procedural framework under Rule 90 relating to verification, reference to the TPO, issuance of invalidity orders, time limits (including deemed validity), consequences of valid exercise, and the manner of electronic filing and verification of form remains broadly unchanged and is substantially aligned with the previous mechanism prescribed under Rule 10TE.

12.2-5b Safe harbour for transactions of provision of information technology services [Rule 91] - Rule 91 of the IT Rules 2026 governs the safe harbour for eligible international transactions of the provision of information technology services. It is not clear whether the application for safe harbour in respect of the provision of data centre services should be made under Rule 90 or 91.

In clause (a) of Rule 87(1), it is provided that an eligible assessee is a person who is engaged in providing information technology services, which consist of any one or more of the following:

(a)

Software development services;

(b)

Information technology-enabled services;

(c)

Knowledge process outsourcing services;

(d)

Contract research and development services wholly or partly relating to software development.

Clause (g) of Rule 87(1) provides that an eligible assessee who has provided data centre services to a foreign company. The separate clauses indicate that information technology services do not cover data centre services. Thus, the application for safe harbour by an eligible assessee should be filed as per Rule 90, which does not seem logical, as Rule 91 covers all information technology-related services, which, to some extent, encompass data centre services. Thus, it is recommended that the Board extend Rule 91 to the data centre services.

To opt for safe harbour in respect of information technology services, the assessee is required to furnish the same Form No. 49. Such form must be filed at any time during the first of the five consecutive tax years for which option for safe harbour is proposed to be exercised and up to the 30th of June of the financial year immediately succeeding the aforesaid first tax year.

2.8-1 What location should the non-resident operate from?

Unlike sections 44BB and 44BBB, section 44BBD requires that the non-resident should be engaged in the business of providing services or technology in India, which could mean three possible scenarios as mentioned below:

(a)

The services are provided in India from overseas,

(b)

The services are provided in India from India,

(c)

The services are provided in India for overseas business.

As discussed in Para 2.4-2g, a position may be taken that the presumptive tax scheme will apply only when the services are provided in India for an Indian business. Where the non-resident is providing services from outside India or providing services from India for an overseas business, the presumptive tax scheme will not be available.

Section 44BBD is silent on how the non-resident should provide these services or technology to a resident company. Thus, the non-resident can provide these services through:

(a)

A fixed place

(b)

The physical presence of his employees in India

(c)

Through his dependent agents in India

A non-resident provider services through dependent agents may fulfil the required conditions because the amount paid or payable to any person on behalf of such a non-resident is considered when computing the presumptive income.

When a non-resident provides services through an independent agent48 or a liaison office49, it may not be considered as providing services in India because of the following reasons:

(a)

A liaison office is not allowed under the FEMA Regulations to carry on any business activity in India. It cannot take any trading, commercial or industrial activity.

(b)

An independent agent is legally and economically independent from his principal. He is responsible to his principal for the results of his work but is not subject to significant control over the manner in which that work is carried out or detailed instructions on how to conduct it.

Furthermore, where some of the services are provided from outside India while some are provided from within India, in our opinion, in genuine cases, the authorities may adopt a lenient approach permitting the presumptive tax scheme, provided that all other conditions are met.

Vodafone's case - It has been held that section 9(1)(i), by a process of interpretation, cannot be extended to cover indirect transfers of capital assets situate in India. To do so, would amount to changing the content and ambit of section 9(1)(i). Since section 9(1)(i) applies to transfers of a capital asset situate in India, therefore, if indirect transfer of a capital asset is read into section 9(1)(i), then the words capital asset situate in India would be rendered nugatory. The meaning of the words 'either directly or indirectly', when read textually and contextually, would indicate that they govern the words those precede them, namely the words 'all income accruing or arising'. The section provides that all income accruing or arising, whether directly or indirectly, would fall within the category of income that is deemed to accrue or arise in India. Thus, the words "directly or indirectly" in section 9(1)(i) go with the income and not with the transfer of a capital asset (property). The question of providing "look through" in the statute or in the treaty is a matter of policy. It is to be expressly provided for in the statute or in the treaty. Similarly, limitation of benefits has to be expressly provided for in the treaty. Such clauses cannot be read into the section by interpretation. Hence, it has been held that section 9(1)(i) is not a "look through" provision.

2.8-1 What location should the non-resident operate from?

Unlike sections 44BB and 44BBB, section 44BBD requires that the non-resident should be engaged in the business of providing services or technology in India, which could mean three possible scenarios as men-tioned below:

(a)

The services are provided in India from overseas,

(b)

The services are provided in India from India,

(c)

The services are provided in India for overseas business.

As discussed in Para 2.4-2g, a position may be taken that the presumptive tax scheme will apply only when the services are provided in India for an Indian business. Where the non-resident is providing services from outside India or providing services from India for an overseas business, the presumptive tax scheme will not be available.

Section 44BBD is silent on how the non-resident should provide these services or technology to a resident company. Thus, the non-resident can provide these services through:

(a)

A fixed place

(b)

The physical presence of his employees in India

(c)

Through his dependent agents in India

A non-resident provider services through dependent agents may fulfil the required conditions because the amount paid or payable to any person on behalf of such a non-resident is considered when computing the presumptive income.

When a non-resident provides services through an independent agent48 or a liaison office49, it may not be considered as providing services in India because of the following reasons:

(a)

A liaison office is not allowed under the FEMA Regulations to carry on any business activity in India. It cannot take any trading, commercial or industrial activity.

(b)

An independent agent is legally and economically independent from his principal. He is responsible to his principal for the results of his work but is not subject to significant control over the manner in which that work is carried out or detailed instructions on how to conduct it.

Furthermore, where some of the services are provided from outside India while some are provided from within India, in our opinion, in genuine cases, the authorities may adopt a lenient approach permitting the presumptive tax scheme, provided that all other conditions are met.

The two independent enterprises must be two unrelated parties having no connection. It does not matter whether the comparables are domestic enterprises or not. However, and it is manifest that the comparable should have similar rights, if any, as the tested party in the brand name, trademark, etc.. As a general rule, the tested party is the one to which a TP method can be applied in the most reliable manner and for which the most reliable comparables can be found, i.e., it will most often be one that has the less complex functional analysis. When applying RPM, CPM or TNMM, it is necessary to choose the party to the transaction for which a financial indicator is tested. In Virtusa Consulting Services (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2021] 124 taxmann.com 309/282 Taxman 95 (Mad.), it has been held that normally, the tested party should be the least complex party to the controlled transaction and there is no bar for selection of tested party either local or foreign party and neither the 1961 Act nor the TP Guidelines provides so and the selection of the tested party is to further the object of the comparability analysis by making it less complex and requiring fewer adjustment. Thus, where the assessee-company was a more complex entity when compared to its foreign AE, said foreign AE could also be selected as a tested party. Also see, PCIT v. Almatis Alumina (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 202/286 Taxman 378 (Cal.).

The tested party normally should be the party in respect of which reliable data for comparison is easily and readily available and fewest adjustments in computations are needed. It may be local or foreign entity, i.e., one party to the transaction. Generally, least of the complex controlled taxpayer should be taken as a tested party. But where comparable or almost comparable, controlled and uncontrolled transactions or entities are available, it may not be right to eliminate them from consideration because they look to be complex. If the taxpayer wishes to take foreign AE as a tested party, then it must ensure that it is such an entity for which the relevant data for comparison is available in public domain or is furnished to the tax administration. The taxpayer is not then entitled to take a stand that such data cannot be called for or insisted upon from the taxpayer—Ranbaxy Laboratories Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2008] 110 ITD 428/167 Taxman 30 (Delhi-Trib).

A functional analysis of the tested party or the independent enterprise, as the case may be, is required to determine whether the transactions are comparable and the adjustments are required to be made to obtain reliable results. The tested party would have to consider other factors, like cost of assets of comparable companies, etc., while applying the return on assets measure. Ordinarily, the tested party has to be the party providing services because it is on the basis of rate of return on sales or cost or operating assets that transactional margin is computed. These parameters are generally available in the case of a party providing services—Aztec Software & Technology Services Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2007] 107 ITD 141/162 Taxman 119/15 SOT 49 (Bang. - Trib.) (SB).

10A.5-2 Number of comparables required - Under the Transfer Pricing Regulations, the number of comparables may be one or more than one; but there is no upper limit prescribed u/s 92C. Therefore, the size of number of comparables has not been prescribed under the provisions of TP Regulations provided under the Income-tax Act. There cannot be a fixed criteria or parameter for number of comparables, which can be universally applied to each and every case for determination of the ALP. It is an accepted rule of sampling that larger size of sample would better and adequate represent the lot or population to which the sample belongs. Therefore, to get an adequate result and better representation, the size of sample must be large enough. The same rule is applicable in the case of number of comparables selected for representing the true and correct ALP in relation to the international transaction. The endeavour should be made to bring more and more comparables so that a proper and realistic price can be determined which represents the price prevailing in the open market. Where the number of comparables available is large, then it is always better to consider as many as possible number of comparables which can give an adequate and proper representation of the price prevailing in open market in the said industry, business, trade etc., to which the comparables and international transactions belong.

10A.5-3 Appropriate set of comparables for profit-based methods - Some of the filters which can be applied while carrying out search for comparables:—

(a)

Availability of financial data - Select only those companies for which the financial information for the period under consideration is available.

(b)

Industry selection - Make a proper selection of the industry heads, e.g., in case the assessee is into manufacturing of auto components, one should ensure that all the industry heads which could possibly have the manufacturing companies of auto components under it should be selected.

[2019] 104 taxmann.com 386/264 Taxman 257 (Bom.), SLP dismissed in PCIT v. L & T Valves Ltd. [2023] 155 taxmann.com 489/295 Taxman 585 (SC)]. Onus - The primary onus to determine the ALP is that of the assessee by resorting to any of the methods prescribed u/s 92C(1) which needs to be most appropriate method (MAM) as per s. 92C(2). Where such onus/burden is discharged by the assessee and the data used for determining the ALP is reliable and correct, there should normally be no intervention by the AO. Ordinarily, it is only where the assessee has not discharged the onus placed on him, or he has not determined the price of the international transaction in terms of the provisions, or the data used by him is not reliable, correct or appropriate, or the TPO finds evidence which discredits the data used by the assessee, or the methodology applied by him in arriving at ALP of the international transaction, the ALP declared by the assessee should be rejected and re-determined in terms of s. 92C [Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2010] 192 Taxman 317 (Delhi)].

Bad debts, not a relevant fact in determining ALP - Merely because assessee has paid royalty even in respect of the products sold by it to the clients, who had not paid for the same, it would make no difference to the determination of the ALP of the transaction since s. 92C provides the basis for determining the ALP and does not either expressly or impliedly consider failure of the assessee's customers to pay for the products sold to them to be a relevant factor in determining the ALP [CIT v. CA Computer Associates India (P.) Ltd. [2012] 25 taxmann.com 22/209 Taxman 382 (Bom.)].

COMPARABILITY

Benchmarking when can be reliable - In order for the benchmarking studies to be reliable for the purposes of determining the ALP, it would be essential that the entities selected as comparables are functionally similar and are subject to the similar business environment and risks as the tested party. In order to impute an ALP to a controlled transaction, it would be essential to ensure that the instances of uncontrolled entities/transactions selected as comparables are similar in all material aspects that have any bearing on the value or the profitability, as the case may be, of the transaction. Any factor, which has an influence on the PLI, would be material and it would be necessary to ensure that the comparables are also equally subjected to the influence of such factors as the tested party. This would, obviously, include business environment, nature and functions performed by the tested party and the comparable entities, value addition in respect of products and services provided by parties, business model, and the assets and resources employed. It cannot be disputed that the functions performed by an entity would have a material bearing on the value and profitability of the entity. It is, therefore, obvious that the comparables selected and the tested party must be functionally similar for ascertaining a reliable ALP [Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 60 taxmann.com 355/234 Taxman 573 (Delhi), SLP granted inCIT v. Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. [2016] 76 taxmann.com 287/[2017] 244 Taxman 153 (SC)].

Comparison allowed with foreign parties also - The assertion that comparison can be made by choosing comparable of domestic cases not using any foreign brand is contrary to the provisions and amounts to rewriting of law. The two independent enterprises must be two unrelated parties having no connection. It does not matter whether the comparables are domestic enterprises or not [Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 55 taxmann.com 240/231 Taxman 113 (Delhi)]. Also see, Virtusa Consulting Services (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 124 taxmann.com 309/282 Taxman 95 (Mad.), followed inPCIT v. Almatis Alumina (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 202/286 Taxman 378 (Cal.).

Data for comparison - While determining comparability of transactions, multiple year data can only be included in manner provided in above Rule 10B(4) and, thus, it is not open to assessee to rely upon PY's data as a general rule [Chryscapital Investment Advisors (India) (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2015] 56 taxmann.com 417/232 Taxman 20 (Delhi)].

8.7-8 Foreign co. does not own or operate physical infrastructure or resources

The exemption will be available to the foreign company, provided it does not own or operate any physical infrastructure or resources of the specified data centre. The combined reading of the definition of 'data centre' and 'data centre services' indicates that the foreign company cannot have ownership or cannot operate the following:

Physical infrastructure (land or buildings)

Power equipment

Cooling system

Security

Information technology infrastructure

Servers

Computers

Storage systems

Operating systems

Security solutions

Network and associated software platforms

Human resources

However, the foreign company can provide value-added software and service layers on top of the Indian data centre's physical infrastructure without owning or operating it. The services typically fall into several categories:

Cloud management and orchestration platforms (providing proprietary portals, APIs, and self-service interfaces for managing resources),

Managed services (offering 24/7 monitoring, performance optimisation, and expert technical support)

Specialised platforms (such as databases, disaster recovery orchestration, industry-specific solutions, security and compliance tools, data analytics and AI/ML platforms, DevOps automation, backup management software, and content delivery network management).

In each case, the Indian company can own and operate the data centre, while the foreign company provides the intelligent software layer, technical expertise, and managed services that make this infrastructure valuable and accessible to end users. The customer interacts with the foreign company's platform and receives comprehensive managed services, but all the underlying physical resources are owned and operated by the Indian data centre. In this case, the foreign company earns its margin from the intellectual property and expertise layer it provides on top of the Indian infrastructure.

8.7-9 Sales to users located in India are made through a reseller entity

The exemption for the foreign company will apply if all sales by the foreign company to users in India are made through a reseller that is an Indian company. This condition indicates that the:

Sales to users in India should be made through the Indian reseller. Sales to overseas users can be done directly by the foreign company. However, the question of exemption from such income does not arise as this income is not deemed to accrue or arise in India [see Para 8.7-11].

(b)

The Indian reseller may be the same as or different from the Indian company operating the data centre.

(c)

The Indian reseller may also be a subsidiary of a foreign company.

2.2 Presumptive taxation regime The words "presumptive basis" are used in the marginal notes of sections 44AD and 44ADA. Though the marginal note of section 44BBD does not use these words, the Explanatory Memorandum to the Finance Bill, 2025, describes section 44BBD as a "Scheme of presumptive taxation extended for non-resident providing services for electronics manufacturing facility".

There is no definition of "presumptive taxation" in any provision of the Act. It is a simplified taxation system that departs from the standard/regular system of starting with the net profit as per the books of account maintained by the assessee and making various allowances and disallowances under the regular provisions of Chapter IV-D of the Act.

Ehtisham Ahmad & Nicholas Stern, in "The Theory and Practice of Tax Reform in Developing Countries" define "Presumptive Taxation" as follows:

"The term presumptive taxation covers a number of procedures under which the 'desired' base for taxation (direct or indirect) is not itself measured but is inferred from some simple indicators which are more easily measured than the base itself."

Victor Thuronyi, in "Presumptive Taxation of the Hard to Tax", defines 'Presumptive Taxation' as under :

"Presumptive taxation involves the use of indirect means to ascertain tax liability, which differ from the usual rules based on the taxpayer's accounts. The term 'presumptive' is used to indicate that there is a legal presumption that the taxpayer's income is not less than the amount resulting from the application of the indirect method."

Presumptive tax provisions are of two types:

(a)

a presumptive tax based on a rebuttable presumption that income/profit from a business is not less than that presumed by the provision based on observable indicators like gross receipts/turnover/capacity. The assessee can rebut the presumption and claim that his profit is lower than the amount presumed under the Section by maintaining accounts and getting them audited under section 44AB;

(b)

a presumptive tax based on an irrebuttable presumption that income/profit from a business is what is presumed under the section based on observable indicators. Here, the assessee cannot claim or prove that his actual profit is less than the amount presumed under the section.

Examples of type (a) presumptive taxation schemes are sections 44AD, 44ADA, 44AE, 44BB and 44BBB. Sections 44B, 44BBA, 44BBC and 44BBD are examples of the type (b) presumptive taxation based on irrebuttable presumptions.

2.3 The non obstante clause overriding sections 28 to 43A

Section 44BBD is expressed to operate notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in sections 28 to 43A. Thus, it does not override sections other than those under sections 28 to 43A, including section 43CB/section 145(2) under which ICDSs are notified.
